title: Managing farrowing problems
subtitle: Most farrowings go smoothly and need nothing from you. The ones that don't move quickly.
excerpt: A healthy sow with a normal litter delivers one piglet roughly every 15-30 minutes. If the interval stretches past an hour between deliveries and the sow is clearly straining, something is wrong. Here is how to recognise a problem presentation, when to assist, and when to call the vet.
sourceNotes: DEFRA Codes of Recommendations for the Welfare of Pigs, farrowing section. AHDB Pork, farrowing management and piglet survival factsheet. John Seymour, The New Complete Book of Self-Sufficiency (2003), breeding and farrowing chapter. Carla Emery, Encyclopedia of Country Living (1994), pig farrowing notes.

glossaryTerms.definition: The process of a sow giving birth. A typical litter is 8–14 piglets, delivered over 2–4 hours. Piglets are born head-first or feet-first with roughly equal frequency.

A piglet positioned at the cervix in a way that blocks delivery. Common examples: both front feet tucked back, hindquarters presented but tail turned sideways, or a very large single piglet spanning the birth canal.
A failure of the uterus to contract effectively during farrowing. The sow may show early signs of labour but then stop progressing, with no deliveries despite obvious piglets still present.

content.text: without needing anything from you except a clean, draught-free pen and a check every 30 minutes. The pattern to watch is the interval between deliveries. Under 30 minutes is normal. Over 60 minutes with a sow who is clearly straining means action is needed.
Sow becomes restless and begins nesting behaviour 12-24 hours before farrowing.
Milk can be expressed from the teats 12-24 hours before farrowing begins.
First piglet arrives after initial active straining. Subsequent piglets follow every 15-30 minutes.

Placenta expelled within 4 hours of the last piglet. A retained placenta in pigs is less critical than in sheep but should still pass; call the vet if it has not appeared 6 hours after the last birth.
Slow delivery: more than 60 minutes between piglets

: gently massage the sow's flank and udder area with your hand. This sometimes restarts contractions. If she is pushing hard with no delivery after 20-25 minutes of observation, consider a manual check. If you are not experienced with manual pig obstetrics, this is a vet call.

attrs.title: Manual assistance — for experienced handlers only

content.text: If you are going to check manually: clean the vulva with warm water, apply obstetric lubricant to your gloved hand and forearm. Work one hand into the birth canal during a contraction. Feel for a piglet at the cervix. If you can identify the head, hook two fingers behind the ears and draw forward gently with each contraction, never between contractions. If you cannot identify a presenting part, do not probe further. Call the vet.

stops delivery and exhausts the sow. Common findings on manual check: a piglet presented head-first but with one or both legs tucked back (normal presentation is head forward and front legs together). Cup the piglet's head, push back slightly, locate the tucked leg, bring it forward. Then draw the piglet out with the next contraction.
Looking after the piglets during farrowing

Each piglet arrives in a sac that usually ruptures on delivery. If it does not, clear the membrane from the nose and mouth immediately. Rub the piglet vigorously with a dry towel, clear the nostrils, and place it under the heat lamp to dry and warm. Ensure each piglet gets to the udder within an hour of birth; the colostrum window is critical in the first six hours.

attrs.cue: No delivery after 2 hours of active straining
attrs.fix: Vet call. Oxytocin injections and manual assistance may be needed. Do not wait.

attrs.cue: Sow becomes very weak between deliveries and stops straining
attrs.cause: Exhaustion or secondary uterine inertia partway through a large litter
attrs.fix: Keep her hydrated with a bucket of warm water. Vet may administer oxytocin to restart contractions. Rest time between piglets can extend to 2 hours in a sow nearing the end of a large litter without this being an emergency, if she is otherwise calm and comfortable.

attrs.cue: Green, foul-smelling discharge during or after farrowing
attrs.cause: Uterine infection or retained dead piglet
attrs.fix: Vet call. Do not administer antibiotics without veterinary direction on dose and duration.
